steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Software developers often face complex technical challenges, and for different reasons they get around them with spurious design workarounds and sub-optimal implementations. These compromises are likely to cause a significant amount of Technical Debt (TD), which means low-quality artefacts that can impair the future maintenance and evolution of the system that is being developed. The current literature reports different types of TD, including code, design, requirements, and documentation. If TD is not identified in time and managed properly, it can cause extra work in the long term, and also additional costs. So it is seen as a critical issue for software development and it is considered ubiquitous in most software projects across all industry segments.

## Motivation

Security issues are closely related to TD, since they are often grounded in quality compromises in the software that is being built. Simple coding mistakes and design flaws can lead to exploitable vulnerabilities that need a lot of time and effort to repair later. Also, like TD, security causes extra costs, because it is often seen as an “after-thought” and not as an actual priority in the software development life cycle. So recent studies have started to look at the intersection between TD and security, with the aim of detecting and managing vulnerabilities in both code and the core architecture of information systems. That is, to use TD as a security indicator and for automatically detecting code vulnerabilities. Still, this research landscape is in its infancy and more investigations are needed at the interface of TD and software security.

A significant part of TD is reported explicitly by developers themselves as “self-admissions”, namely through software artefacts like code comments. Also, recent studies have looked at commit messages and pull requests as valuable sources of Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SATD). These artefacts have been central for analysing different TD types beyond code, including requirement debt and documentation debt. But SATD sources can also have major security implications when they report flaws and vulnerabilities in the software. In particular, an attacker could use security pointers disclosed inside these sources (e.g., a code comment like ‘‘TODO: Make it thread-safe’’) to spot exploitable weaknesses in the system that threaten its availability, confidentiality and integrity. Even though this is important, as far as we know the security implications of SATD have not been investigated or documented in the literature.

## Contribution and Research Questions
- Focus: security pointers in SATD across code comments, commits, issue reports, pull requests; OSS (public artefacts -> easy targets); mixed methods (repository data + online survey)
- RQ1: 8,812 SATD instances (preexisting dataset) -> keyword search, 546 candidates -> manual inspection, 201 SSATD
- RQ2: mapped to CWE; 25 CWE types; 8 among MITRE’s Top-25 (2023)
- RQ3: survey, 222 participants; many disclose despite risk; nine motives (‘promote a security culture’), three risks (‘security misconceptions’)
- Organisation: Sections 2–7

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Software developers often face complex technical challenges, and for different reasons they get around them with spurious design workarounds and sub-optimal implementations. ## Motivation

Security issues are closely related to TD, since they are often grounded in quality compromises in the software that is being built. Simple coding mistakes and design flaws can lead to exploitable vulnerabilities that need a lot of time and effort to repair later. Also, like TD, security causes extra costs, because it is often seen as an “after-thought” and not as an actual priority in the software development life cycle. So recent studies have started to look at the intersection between TD and security, with the aim of detecting and managing vulnerabilities in both code and the core architecture of information systems. That is, to use TD as a security indicator and for automatically detecting code vulnerabilities. Still, this research landscape is in its infancy and more investigations are needed at the interface of TD and software security.

A significant part of TD is reported explicitly by developers themselves as “self-admissions”, namely through software artefacts like code comments. Also, recent studies have looked at commit messages and pull requests as valuable sources of Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SATD). These artefacts have been central for analysing different TD types beyond code, including requirement debt and documentation debt. But SATD sources can also have major security implications when they report flaws and vulnerabilities in the software. In particular, an attacker could use security pointers disclosed inside these sources (e.g., a code comment like ‘‘TODO: Make it thread-safe’’) to spot exploitable weaknesses in the system that threaten its availability, confidentiality and integrity. Even though this is important, as far as we know the security implications of SATD have not been investigated or documented in the literature.

## Contribution and Research Questions

This work looks at the implications of security pointers inside SATD instances across multiple sources. In particular, it investigates whether explicit references to security vulnerabilities inside code comments, commits, issue reports, and pull requests can help to characterise exploitable weaknesses inside Open-Source Software (OSS). We focused on OSS projects and repositories because they become easy targets of security attacks by making their artefacts visible and available to the general public. We did a mixed-methods analysis of data extracted from OSS repositories and a complementary online survey to address the following Research Questions (RQs):

- RQ1: Can SATD sources contain pointers to security weaknesses and vulnerabilities inside OSS repositories? To answer this RQ we analysed a preexisting dataset containing 8,812 SATD instances from multiple sources. With a keyword-based search we extracted 546 security-relevant SATD candidates and inspected them manually for security pointers. As a result we gathered 201 Security Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SSATD) observations, which we considered for further analysis.

- RQ2: Which particular weakness and vulnerabilities are frequently exposed through different SATD sources? For this RQ we mapped each SSATD instance in our resulting dataset manually to Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) identifiers. Overall we identified 25 different CWE types across commit messages, code comments, pull requests, and issue reports. Also, 8 of these 25 CWEs are listed among MITRE’s Top-25 most dangerous software weaknesses in 2023.

- RQ3: What is developers’ perspective on security-related SATD in OSS repositories? We addressed this RQ with an online survey with OSS practitioners. We recruited 222 participants in total and asked them about their tendencies to disclose security pointers inside SATD artefacts, their underlying motivations, and whether they thought this was a risky practice. Our results show that many practitioners do this, although they recognise it as potentially risky. In total we identified nine motives that drive developers to disclose security pointers inside SATD artefacts (e.g., ‘promote a security culture’) and three potential risks that come from them (e.g., ‘security misconceptions’).

The rest of this paper is organised like this. Section 2 gives the background and summarises the related work. Section 3 explains our research methodology, and Section 4 reports the findings. Section 5 reflects on the findings and gives implications for research and practice. Section 6 discusses the possible threats of our study and the mitigation strategies we adopted. Section 7 concludes the paper and discusses some future research directions.
